title: The annunciation and the birth
excerpt: The angels and Maryam, the palm tree, and the infant who speaks.
body: @islamic

The Qur’an tells the story of Maryam and the birth of ʿĪsā twice, and more fully than it tells the birth of any other prophet. Sūrat Āl ʿImrān (3:33-47) sets it in the history of a family: the wife of ʿImrān dedicates her unborn child to God, the child is a girl, Maryam, and she is raised in the sanctuary under the care of Zakariyyā, where the angels announce to her a word from God whose name is the Messiah, ʿĪsā ibn Maryam. Sūrat Maryam (19:16-34), which takes its name from her, tells the birth itself: the withdrawal, the spirit in the form of a man, the palm tree, and the infant who speaks. Together the passages give the Qur’anic account of how he came into the world, and that account is the measure for both gospel nativities.
## Maryam before the annunciation

“Remember when the wife of ʿImrān said, ‘My Lord, I dedicate what is in my womb entirely to Your service, so accept it from me’” (3:35). When the child is born a girl, her mother names her Maryam and asks God’s protection for her and her offspring from Satan (3:36). God accepts her “with gracious acceptance” and makes her grow in goodness; Zakariyyā is given charge of her, and every time he enters her sanctuary he finds her provided with food, which she says is from God (3:37). The angels tell her that God has chosen her and purified her and chosen her above the women of the worlds (3:42).

None of this is in the four gospels, which begin Mary’s story at the annunciation. It is in the Protevangelium of James, a Christian text of the second century, which tells of Mary’s dedication by her mother, her upbringing in the Temple and her being fed by an angel. The Qur’an and that text share a tradition about Mary that the canonical gospels left out.
## The announcement

In 3:45-47 the angels speak: “O Maryam, God gives you good news of a word from Him, whose name is the Messiah, ʿĪsā son of Maryam, held in honour in this world and the next, and one of those brought near. He will speak to people in the cradle and in maturity, and he will be of the righteous.” She asks how she can have a child when no man has touched her, and the answer is: “So it will be. God creates what He wills; when He decrees a matter, He only says to it ‘Be’, and it is” (3:47).

In 19:16-21 the scene is told again, alone. She withdraws from her people to a place in the east and screens herself; God sends His spirit to her, and it takes the form of a well-made man; she takes refuge in God from him; he says he is only a messenger of her Lord, to give her a pure boy; she asks how, since no man has touched her and she has not been unchaste; he answers that it is easy for God, and that the child will be a sign for people and a mercy from God, “and it is a matter decreed” (19:21).

Luke 1:26-38 tells the same scene with the angel named as Gabriel and the child announced as the Son of the Most High who will reign on the throne of David for ever. The Qur’an announces a word from God, a Messiah and a sign; it does not announce a son of God, and that difference is the whole difference between the Qur’an and the gospel.
## The birth

“So she conceived him and withdrew with him to a distant place. The pains of labour drove her to the trunk of a palm tree. She said, ‘I wish I had died before this and been a thing forgotten.’ Then a voice called to her from below her: ‘Do not grieve. Your Lord has placed a stream beneath you. Shake the trunk of the palm towards you and it will drop fresh ripe dates upon you. So eat and drink and be comforted’” (19:22-26).

There is no Bethlehem, no inn, no manger, no shepherds and no magi. The palm tree is absent from Matthew and Luke and appears in the Gospel of Pseudo-Matthew, a Latin text of the sixth or seventh century, where the child Jesus on the flight to Egypt commands a palm to bend and give his mother its fruit, and a spring to rise at its roots.
Which tradition is older is an open question; the Qur’an sets the palm at the birth, Pseudo-Matthew on the road to Egypt.
## The infant speaks

Maryam brings the child to her people, who accuse her: “O sister of Hārūn, your father was not a bad man, nor was your mother unchaste” (19:28). She points to the child. They say, “How can we speak to one who is in the cradle, a child?” And he speaks: “I am the servant of God. He has given me the Book and made me a prophet. He has made me blessed wherever I am, and enjoined on me prayer and almsgiving as long as I live, and kindness to my mother; He has not made me arrogant or wretched. Peace be upon me the day I was born, the day I die, and the day I am raised alive” (19:30-33).

The speech is at once a defence of his mother and a statement, in his first words, of what he is: a servant, a prophet, a man of prayer and alms. The Qur’an then adds its own comment: “That is ʿĪsā son of Maryam, the word of truth about which they dispute. It is not for God to take a son; glory be to Him” (19:34-35).

The speaking infant appears in the Arabic Infancy Gospel, a text later than the Qur’an, where Jesus in the cradle tells his mother that he is the Son of God. The Qur’an has him say the opposite. The charge that the Qur’an confuses this Maryam with the sister of Moses is answered in Ezra and Mary in the Qur’an at Best of Islam.
## What the Qur’an does not say

It does not name Joseph or give Maryam a husband, and it places the birth in no named town, Bethlehem included. It has no census, no star, no massacre, no flight into Egypt and no genealogy. Where the gospel nativities contradict each other (see the discrepancy tables), the Qur’an takes neither side, because it tells a different story with a different purpose: to show a sign of God’s power to create without a father, as He created Ādam without one (3:59). Descent from David plays no part in it.
## Compare

Matthew 1-2 and Luke 1-2 agree with the Qur’an that Maryam was a virgin, that the conception was announced by a messenger from God, and that the child was a sign. They differ from it in what the sign meant. In the Qur’an the virgin birth is a proof of God’s creative word, and the Qur’an says so in the same breath (3:47; 3:59; 19:35); it proves nothing about a divine nature in the child. The Gospel According to Islam on this website follows the Qur’anic account in section 2, and the Qur’anic text itself stands there under its own heading.
## Sources
- Ṭabarī, Jāmiʿ al-bayān, on 3:33-47 and 19:16-34.
- Gabriel Said Reynolds, The Qur’ān and Its Biblical Subtext, chapters on Mary.

- Suleiman Mourad, “From Hellenism to Christianity and Islam: The Origin of the Palm Tree Story concerning Mary and Jesus in the Gospel of Pseudo-Matthew and the Qur’ān”, Oriens Christianus 86 (2002).
- Bart Ehrman and Zlatko Pleše, The Apocryphal Gospels: Texts and Translations, for the Protevangelium of James and Pseudo-Matthew.

title: The signs
excerpt: The bird of clay, the blind and the leper healed, the dead raised, by the permission of God.
body: @islamic

Twice the Qur’an lists the signs given to ʿĪsā: once in the angels’ announcement to Maryam (3:49) and once in God’s own words to him on the Day of Judgement (5:110). The lists are nearly the same, and in both of them one phrase is repeated after almost every sign: “by God’s permission” (bi-idhni llāh). That phrase is the key to how the Qur’an reads the miracle stories of the gospels, and it is the measure this website applies to them.
## Both lists

3:49: “I have come to you with a sign from your Lord. I will make for you from clay the shape of a bird, then breathe into it, and it will become a bird by God’s permission. I will heal the blind from birth and the leper, and I will give life to the dead, by God’s permission. And I will tell you what you eat and what you store in your houses. Surely in that is a sign for you, if you are believers.”

5:110: “O ʿĪsā son of Maryam, remember My favour upon you and upon your mother, when I strengthened you with the holy spirit so that you spoke to people in the cradle and in maturity; when I taught you the Book and wisdom, the Torah and the Injīl; when you made from clay the shape of a bird by My permission, then breathed into it and it became a bird by My permission; when you healed the blind from birth and the leper by My permission; when you brought out the dead by My permission; and when I held back the Children of Israel from you, when you came to them with clear signs and those who disbelieved among them said, ‘This is nothing but plain sorcery.’”
## The signs one by one

- The bird of clay. He shapes a bird from clay, breathes into it, and it lives. The gospels have no such story. It is in the Infancy Gospel of Thomas, a Greek text of the second century, where the child Jesus makes 12 sparrows from clay on the sabbath and claps his hands to send them flying (2:1-5). The Qur’an takes the story out of a child’s game and makes it a sign given to the messenger, and adds the words the infancy gospel does not have: by God’s permission.

- The blind and the leper. The healing of the blind (Mark 8:22-26; 10:46-52; John 9) and of lepers (Mark 1:40-45; Luke 17:11-19) runs through all four gospels. The Qur’an specifies the blind from birth (akmah), which is the case of John 9, where the disciples ask whose sin caused it and Jesus answers that it was so that the works of God might be shown in him (9:3).

- The dead raised. The gospels record 3: the daughter of Jairus (Mark 5:35-43), the widow’s son at Nain (Luke 7:11-17) and Lazarus (John 11). In every case the gospels, like the Qur’an, show Jesus praying or acting under God; at the tomb of Lazarus he says aloud, “Father, I thank you for having heard me” (John 11:41).
- What they eat and store. Only 3:49 has this, and it has no gospel parallel. The classical commentators read it of knowledge given him by God of what was hidden, a prophet’s gift like that of Yūsuf.
- Speech in the cradle, in 5:110 and 3:46, is the sign told in full at 19:29-33; see the annunciation and the birth.
## The refrain

Seven times across both passages the Qur’an says the sign was by God’s permission. The gospels agree: Jesus did his works by the finger of God (Luke 11:20), the crowds glorified God, “who had given such authority to human beings” (Matthew 9:8), and Peter in Acts calls him “a man attested to you by God with deeds of power, wonders, and signs that God did through him” (Acts 2:22).
The later church read the miracles as proof of his divinity. The Qur’an and the earliest preaching read them as proof of his mission: God did them, through him, for a people who asked for a sign.
The refrain corrects how the record was read. Every sign the gospels give him the Qur’an gives him too, and it gives him one more; what it withholds is the inference.
## “Plain sorcery”

The second passage ends with the response of those who disbelieved: that this was plain sorcery (5:110); the first ends with the signs offered “if you are believers” (3:49), and the Qur’an says that they plotted against him (3:54). The gospels record the same charge in the same words: “By the ruler of the demons he casts out demons” (Mark 3:22), and the same answer, that a kingdom divided against itself cannot stand. The Gospel According to Islam places that exchange in section 14, with the bird of clay beside it.
## Why it matters here

The signs are the point at which the gospels and the Qur’an are closest in matter and furthest in meaning. The gospels record more signs than the Qur’an lists: water into wine, the calming of the storm, the walking on the sea, the feeding of the multitudes. The Qur’an names the healings, the raisings and the bird of clay, and leaves the rest where the measure leaves everything it is silent on: kept if early, and marked as such.

What both books share, the healings and raisings and the charge of sorcery, they read differently: in one a man through whom God acted, in the other, by the time the creeds were written, God himself acting. The Qur’an’s phrase settles which reading the gospels’ own words support.
A servant does signs by permission. The one who gives permission does not need it.
## Sources
- Ṭabarī and Ibn Kathīr, commentary on 3:49 and 5:110.
- Gabriel Said Reynolds, The Qur’ān and Its Biblical Subtext.
- Bart Ehrman and Zlatko Pleše, The Apocryphal Gospels, for the Infancy Gospel of Thomas.
- Tarif Khalidi, The Muslim Jesus: Sayings and Stories in Islamic Literature.

title: The Messiah in Islam: a servant and a messenger
excerpt: Who is the Messiah in Islam? The Qur’an gives ʿĪsā son of Maryam the title al-Masīḥ 11 times, and calls him a servant, a prophet and a messenger of God.
body: @islamic

The Qur’an gives ʿĪsā more titles than it gives any other prophet, and it is as careful about what it denies him as about what it grants. He is a servant, a prophet and a messenger; the Messiah; a word from God and a spirit from Him; a sign and a mercy; one of those brought near. He is not God, not the son of God, and not one of three.
## What he is

- A servant of God (ʿabd Allāh). His own first words: “I am the servant of God” (19:30). “The Messiah would never disdain to be a servant of God, nor would the angels brought near” (4:172). “He was no more than a servant on whom We bestowed favour, and We made him an example for the Children of Israel” (43:59).

- A prophet and a messenger. “He has made me a prophet” (19:30). “A messenger to the Children of Israel” (3:49). “The Messiah, son of Maryam, was no more than a messenger; messengers had passed away before him. His mother was a woman of truth. They both ate food” (5:75). “ʿĪsā son of Maryam said, ‘O Children of Israel, I am the messenger of God to you’” (61:6).
- The Messiah (al-Masīḥ), 11 times in 9 verses, 7 of them joining the title to “son of Maryam”. The Qur’an uses the title without explaining it, as a name his people knew.

- A word from God and a spirit from Him. “The Messiah, ʿĪsā son of Maryam, was a messenger of God, and His word which He cast to Maryam, and a spirit from Him” (4:171; compare 3:45). The classical commentators read “word” of the creative command “Be” by which he was conceived without a father (3:47, 3:59), and “spirit from Him” of the breath by which God gives life, as He breathed into Ādam (15:29; 32:9). Neither title is used of him alone: the whole of creation is by God’s word, and every living soul by His spirit.

- A sign and a mercy (19:21; 21:91; 23:50), held in honour in this world and the next, and one of those brought near (3:45), blessed wherever he is (19:31), strengthened with the holy spirit (2:87; 2:253; 5:110), taught the Book and wisdom, the Torah and the Injīl (3:48; 5:110).
## Who is the Messiah in Islam?

In Islam the Messiah is ʿĪsā son of Maryam, Jesus, and no one else. The Qur’an gives the title to him alone, 11 times in 9 verses (3:45; 4:157; 4:171; 4:172; 5:17; 5:72; 5:75; 9:30; 9:31), and the angels give it with his name before he is born: “God gives you good news of a word from Him, whose name is the Messiah, ʿĪsā son of Maryam, held in honour in this world and the next, and one of those brought near” (3:45).

Muḥammad is called the messenger of God and the seal of the prophets (33:40), and never the Messiah. The Mahdī of the reports about the last days is another man again, and the Qur’an does not mention him.
## What “Messiah” means in the Qur’an

Al-Ṭabarī, on 3:45, explains masīḥ as mamsūḥ, “wiped” or “anointed”: God wiped him clean and purified him of sins. He reports from Ibrāhīm al-Nakhaʿī that al-Masīḥ means “the truthful one” (al-ṣiddīq), and from Saʿīd that he was so named because he was anointed with blessing (Jāmiʿ al-bayān, ed. Shākir, reports 7063-7066).

The Arabic word is the Hebrew mashiaḥ, the anointed one, which the Greek gospels translate as Christos. The Qur’an keeps the title and denies what the churches built on it: “The Messiah, son of Maryam, was no more than a messenger” (5:75).
## Are Muslims waiting for the Messiah?

Muslims expect the same ʿĪsā son of Maryam to return before the end of the world. The Prophet said: “By Him in whose hand is my soul, the son of Maryam will soon come down among you as a just judge. He will break the cross, kill the swine and abolish the jizya” (al-Bukhārī 3448). Abū Hurayra, who narrated it, recited 4:159 with it: “there is none of the People of the Book but will believe in him before his death.”

The ḥadīth also name a false messiah, al-masīḥ al-dajjāl, the deceiver of the last days, whom the Prophet described as blind in the right eye (al-Bukhārī 3439). How the Qur’an speaks of his being raised to God is on the end of his earthly mission.
## What he is not

“They have disbelieved who say, ‘God is the Messiah, son of Maryam.’ Say: who could prevent God, if He willed, from destroying the Messiah son of Maryam and his mother and everyone on earth?” (5:17). “They have disbelieved who say, ‘God is the Messiah, son of Maryam,’ when the Messiah himself said, ‘O Children of Israel, worship God, my Lord and your Lord.’ Whoever associates partners with God, God has forbidden him Paradise” (5:72). “They have disbelieved who say, ‘God is the third of three,’ when there is no god but one God” (5:73). “O People of the Book, do not go to excess in your religion, and say nothing of God but the truth. The Messiah, ʿĪsā son of Maryam, was a messenger of God… so believe in God and His messengers, and do not say ‘Three.’ Stop; it is better for you. God is only one God; glory be to Him, that He should have a son” (4:171). “It is not for God to take a son” (19:35). “They say, ‘The Most Merciful has taken a son.’ You have put forward something monstrous” (19:88-89). “He begets not, nor is He begotten” (112:3).

The denials are precise. The Qur’an says that calling God “three” is excess, and that making the Messiah God, or God’s son, is to associate a partner with Him; it nowhere says that Christians worship three gods.

The argument it gives is from his humanity: he and his mother ate food (5:75); God could destroy him (5:17); he was created as Ādam was, from dust, by the word “Be” (3:59). Such a being is a creature, and the Qur’an says so.

The reasons Muslims hold that Jesus is not God are set out in Five reasons Muslims believe Jesus is not God at Best of Islam, and the case that the God of the Qur’an is the God of the Bible in Six reasons there; what the Qur’an says that bears on Paul of Tarsus is read in The Qur’an as witness at Apostle of Doom.
## Why the denials are absolute

The Qur’an’s refusals follow from what God is. “Nothing is like unto Him” (42:11); “if there were gods besides God in the heavens and the earth, both would have fallen into ruin” (21:22); God is one, the ultimate, and whatever is not God is creation.

Al-Fārūqī puts the point as a rule of thought: only one God can be ultimate, and if He is, He must be transcendent, beyond every creature, so that no creature can “represent, personify or in any way express the divine being”. ʿĪsā, who ate food and was made from dust by the word “Be”, is on the creature’s side of that line, and no excellence in him can move him across it.

That is why the Qur’an can honour ʿĪsā with more titles than any other prophet and still say, in the same breath, that it is not for God to take a son. The honour is a creature’s; the oneness is God’s alone (al-Fārūqī, pp. 21-24).
## The final scene

In 5:116-118 the Qur’an sets the question in the mouth of God and the answer in the mouth of ʿĪsā, on the Day of Judgement: “And when God says, ‘O ʿĪsā son of Maryam, did you say to people, “Take me and my mother as two gods besides God”?’ he will say, ‘Glory be to You! It is not for me to say what I have no right to say. If I had said it, You would have known it. You know what is in my soul, and I do not know what is in Yours. You alone know all that is hidden. I said to them only what You commanded me: “Worship God, my Lord and your Lord.” I was a witness over them as long as I was among them, and when You took me, You were the watcher over them, and You are witness over all things. If You punish them, they are Your servants; if You forgive them, You are the Mighty, the Wise.’” The passage is the Qur’an’s own summary of his teaching: worship God, my Lord and your Lord. Everything said of him in his name after he was taken, he disowns.
## Compare
The gospels record the same teaching in his mouth. “Why do you call me good? No one is good but God alone” (Mark 10:18). “Hear, O Israel: the Lord our God, the Lord is one” (Mark 12:29).

“The Father is greater than I” (John 14:28). “I am ascending to my Father and your Father, to my God and your God” (John 20:17). “This is eternal life, that they may know you, the only true God” (John 17:3).
They also record, in the latest of them, the titles the Qur’an denies (see John). The Qur’an keeps the first voice and sets aside the second, and this website does the same on the measure.
## Questions about Jesus and the Messiah in Islam
? Does Islam believe Jesus is the Messiah?

Yes. The Qur’an calls ʿĪsā son of Maryam the Messiah 11 times and gives the title to no one else (3:45; 4:171). It denies only that the title makes him divine: “The Messiah, son of Maryam, was no more than a messenger” (5:75).
? Do Muslims believe in Jesus?

Yes. Belief in him is part of the faith: “Say: we believe in God and what was sent down to us, and what was given to Mūsā and ʿĪsā and to the prophets from their Lord; we make no distinction between any of them” (2:136). The Qur’an counts whoever believes in some messengers and rejects others a disbeliever (4:150-151). Muslims believe in him as a prophet, a messenger and the Messiah, and do not worship him.
? Does the Qur’an say Jesus is God?

It says that those who call God the Messiah have disbelieved, and has the Messiah himself say: “O Children of Israel, worship God, my Lord and your Lord” (5:72; 5:17). He and his mother ate food (5:75).
? Does the Qur’an call Jesus the word of God?
Yes: “His word which He cast to Maryam, and a spirit from Him” (4:171; 3:45). Al-Ṭabarī and Ibn Kathīr read the word as the command “Be” by which he was created without a father (3:47; 3:59).
? Is Jesus the son of God in Islam?

No. “It is not for God to take a son” (19:35); “He begets not, nor is He begotten” (112:3). The Qur’an quotes the saying “the Messiah is the son of God” to reject it (9:30), and his own first words are “I am the servant of God” (19:30).
? What does Messiah mean in Islam?
Anointed, or wiped. Al-Ṭabarī explains al-Masīḥ as the one God wiped clean of sins, and reports that he was anointed with blessing; the word is the Hebrew mashiaḥ, “Christ” in Greek.
? Is Muhammad the Messiah?
No. The Qur’an calls Muḥammad the messenger of God and the seal of the prophets (33:40). The title al-Masīḥ belongs to ʿĪsā son of Maryam alone.
? Do Muslims believe Jesus will come back?

Yes. The Prophet said the son of Maryam will come down as a just judge, break the cross and kill the swine (al-Bukhārī 3448), and the classical commentators read 4:159 and 43:61 of his return before the Hour.
## Sources
- Ṭabarī, Jāmiʿ al-bayān, ed. Maḥmūd Shākir, on 3:45 (reports 7063-7066, the meaning of al-Masīḥ), 4:171-172, 5:72-75 and 5:116-118; Ibn Kathīr on the same verses.
- Al-Bukhārī, al-Ṣaḥīḥ, Kitāb aḥādīth al-anbiyāʾ, 3439 and 3448 (the second under bāb nuzūl ʿĪsā ibn Maryam).
- Geoffrey Parrinder, Jesus in the Qur’ān, chapters on the titles.
- Mahmoud Ayoub, “Towards an Islamic Christology: An Image of Jesus in Early Shiʿi Muslim Literature”, The Muslim World 66 (1976).
- Neal Robinson, Christ in Islam and Christianity.
- Ismāʿīl Rājī al-Fārūqī, Divine Transcendence and Its Expression (Kuala Lumpur: Muslim Youth Movement of Malaysia, 1983), pp. 21-24, on transcendence as the ground of the Qur’anic denials.

title: The table from heaven
excerpt: The disciples ask for a sign, and receive it with a warning.
body: @islamic

The fifth sūra of the Qur’an is called al-Māʾida, “The Table”, after 4 verses near its end (5:112-115) in which the disciples of ʿĪsā ask for a table to be sent down from heaven, and he asks God for it, and God grants it with a warning. It is the only miracle in the Qur’an that the disciples request, and the only one that comes with a threat attached.
## The passage

“When the disciples said, ‘O ʿĪsā son of Maryam, can your Lord send down to us a table from heaven?’ he said, ‘Fear God, if you are believers.’ They said, ‘We wish to eat from it, and to have our hearts set at rest, and to know that you have told us the truth, and to be witnesses to it.’ ʿĪsā son of Maryam said, ‘O God, our Lord, send down to us a table from heaven, to be a festival for us, for the first of us and the last of us, and a sign from You; and provide for us, for You are the best of providers.’ God said, ‘I will send it down to you. But whoever of you disbelieves after that, I will punish him with a punishment I have not inflicted on anyone in the worlds’” (5:112-115).
## The disciples

The disciples (al-ḥawāriyyūn) appear in the Qur’an as the men who answered when ʿĪsā asked, “Who will be my helpers in the way of God?” and who said, “We are God’s helpers; we believe in God; bear witness that we are Muslims” (3:52; 61:14). They are believers, and the Qur’an says God inspired them to believe (5:111).

Their request here comes from belief: they say they want their hearts set at rest, the same words the Qur’an gives Ibrāhīm when he asks to see how God gives life to the dead (2:260). ʿĪsā’s first answer, “Fear God”, is a prophet’s caution against asking for signs; his prayer, once they explain themselves, asks for the table as a festival and a sign, and for provision.

The Qur’an does not say whether the table came down. The commentators are nearly unanimous that it did, and they describe it: fish and bread, fruits of Paradise, a meal that fed the poor and the sick. Mujāhid and al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī held that when the disciples heard the warning they withdrew the request, and that the table never came.
## The warning

The threat in 5:115 is the severest in the Qur’an, and it is attached to a meal. The sense is that a sign asked for and given leaves no excuse: those who disbelieve after seeing it are worse than those who never saw. The gospels say the same of the towns that saw the signs and did not repent: “it will be more tolerable for Tyre and Sidon on the day of judgement than for you” (Matthew 11:21-24). In Shafaat’s telling, the warning is the reason the disciples’ faith is tested so hard afterwards.
## Compare

The table resembles 3 gospel scenes, and the Qur’an names none of them. The feeding of the multitudes (Mark 6:30-44; 8:1-10; John 6:1-14) is a meal from heaven for a crowd, after which the crowd in John asks for a sign “that we may see it and believe you” and is told of the bread from heaven (6:30-33). The Last Supper (Mark 14:22-25; 1 Corinthians 11:23-26) is a meal with the disciples that became the Christian festival, which matches “a festival for the first of us and the last of us”.

Peter’s vision of a sheet let down from heaven with food on it (Acts 10:9-16) is a “table” of a kind, and the word the Qur’an uses, māʾida, is a loanword from Ethiopic, where it was used of the Christian altar table. Each parallel fits part of the passage and none fits the whole.

What the Qur’an has done is to keep the memory of a meal from God that the disciples shared with him and that became their festival, and to strip it of the meaning the church gave it. The meal it keeps has bread from the best of providers and a warning to be grateful, and no body broken or blood poured out.
## Why it matters here

The Last Supper is the root of the Christian sacrament and of the doctrine that his death was a sacrifice. The Qur’an’s table is a feast and a sign, given at the disciples’ request, with no death in it. The Gospel According to Islam sets the table in section 16, before Caesarea Philippi, and the last supper in section 23, where the words over the bread and the cup are given as the gospels have them and the note explains how the measure reads them.
## Sources
- Ṭabarī, Jāmiʿ al-bayān, and Ibn Kathīr, Tafsīr, on 5:112-115.
- Gabriel Said Reynolds, The Qur’ān and Its Biblical Subtext, on the table.
- Arthur Jeffery, The Foreign Vocabulary of the Qur’ān, under māʾida.
- Matthias Radscheit, “Table”, in Encyclopaedia of the Qur’ān.

title: The end of his earthly mission
excerpt: Neither killed nor crucified, but raised to God.
body: @islamic
One verse of the Qur’an, 4:157, is the point at which the Muslim and Christian accounts of Jesus part for good. Everything else can be read as difference of emphasis; this is contradiction.

The Christian gospel is that Christ died on the cross and rose. The Qur’an says that he was not killed and not crucified, and that God raised him to Himself. Six facts about the verse, in short form, are in The crucifixion and the Qur’an at Best of Islam.
## The verses

“And for their saying, ‘We killed the Messiah, ʿĪsā son of Maryam, the messenger of God.’ They did not kill him, nor did they crucify him, but it was made to appear so to them (shubbiha lahum). Those who differ about it are in doubt about it; they have no knowledge of it, only the following of conjecture. They certainly did not kill him. Rather, God raised him to Himself. God is Mighty, Wise. There is none of the People of the Book but will believe in him before his death, and on the Day of Resurrection he will be a witness against them” (4:157-159).

The verse answers a boast. The subject is the Jews who rejected him, and the Qur’an denies them the killing: they did not do it, whatever they said. It is in the middle of a list of their offences (4:153-161), and the point is that God protected His messenger from them.
## Related verses

- 3:54-55: “They plotted, and God plotted, and God is the best of plotters. When God said, ‘O ʿĪsā, I will take you (mutawaffīka) and raise you to Myself, and purify you from those who disbelieve, and set those who follow you above those who disbelieve until the Day of Resurrection.’”
- 5:117: “When You took me (tawaffaytanī), You were the watcher over them.”
- 19:33: “Peace be upon me the day I was born, the day I die, and the day I am raised alive”, the infant’s own words, in which death and resurrection are in the future and are his own.
- 4:159, above, read in most of the classical commentaries as a prophecy of his return before the end, when the People of the Book will believe in him as he is.
## How Muslims have read it

The majority view of the classical commentators, from al-Ṭabarī onwards, is that God raised ʿĪsā to heaven alive, that another man was made to look like him and was crucified in his place, and that he will return before the Day of Judgement, as the ḥadīth also say. Who the substitute was, the Qur’an does not say, and the answers have a history of their own, set out below.
On this reading the raising to God is the end of his earthly mission, and his return before the Day of Judgement, which most of the classical commentators find in 4:159, is still to come.

The verb tawaffā in 3:55 and 5:117, which usually means “cause to die”, they read as “take up” or as a sleep. A minority of early commentators, and some modern ones, read tawaffā as death: God caused him to die a natural death, at a time of His choosing, and raised him; what the Jews did not do was kill him. Both readings agree on the one thing the verse states: he was not killed by his enemies and not crucified.

The substitution story is an explanation of “it was made to appear so to them”; the Qur’an itself names no substitute and describes no scene. Early Christian groups said the same thing: Basilides, according to Irenaeus (Against Heresies 1.24.4), taught that Simon of Cyrene was crucified in Jesus’s form, and the Nag Hammadi Apocalypse of Peter and Second Treatise of the Great Seth have the living Jesus laughing above the cross while another suffers.

The Qur’an may be answering a boast with a memory the church had suppressed. Basilides’ account and the crucifixion passages of the Second Treatise of the Great Seth and the Coptic Apocalypse of Peter are woven into section 26 of the gospel on this website, with the measure applied to each.
## How the substitute was identified, and when

The Qur’an names no one, and neither does the ḥadīth. The earliest reports, preserved by al-Ṭabarī (d. 923) on 4:157, make the substitute one of the disciples, who volunteered to take on his likeness and be killed in his place; a second set of reports makes him the man sent into the house to seize Jesus, who came out wearing his face. Both are Muslim stories of the first 2 centuries, and both honour the substitute as a believer or treat him as a culprit caught in his own trap.

Judas Iscariot as the man on the cross belongs to later writing and is above all the plot of the Gospel of Barnabas, a work of Muslim colour that survives only in Italian and Spanish manuscripts of the sixteenth century and has no claim to antiquity. Simon of Cyrene is named by no classical Muslim scholar at all; that identification is Christian, taught by Basilides in the second century and known through Irenaeus, and it entered Muslim apologetics only in modern times, when Muslim writers found it in the church fathers. This website uses it as what it is, an early Christian witness that the one on the cross was another.

A fourth reading, that Jesus was nailed to the cross but did not die on it and was revived in the tomb, was argued by Mirza Ghulam Ahmad in 1899 and popularised by Ahmed Deedat in the 1980s; it does not fit the verse, which denies the crucifixion as well as the killing, and this website does not use it.
## The historical question
@consensus

That Jesus of Nazareth was crucified by order of Pontius Pilate is accepted by nearly all historians of the period, including those with no Christian commitment, as one of the few secure facts about him. It is attested by Paul of Tarsus within 25 years (1 Corinthians 2:2; Galatians 3:1), by all four gospels, by Josephus (Antiquities 18.64, in the part of the passage most scholars accept as genuine) and by Tacitus (Annals 15.44), and it is the kind of fact no follower would have invented, since a crucified Messiah was a contradiction in terms to Jews and an absurdity to Greeks (1 Corinthians 1:23). This website states that consensus plainly, and does not pretend that it is weaker than it is.
## Where this page stands

The historian’s claim and the Qur’an’s are of different kinds. The historian says that a man was nailed to a cross in Jerusalem in about 30 CE and that the people who were there believed him to be Jesus. The Qur’an says that whatever they believed, God did not let His messenger be killed by his enemies, and that the matter was made to appear otherwise to them.

The second claim is not open to the historian’s methods, because it concerns what God did, and the Qur’an says in the same verse that those who argue about it are following conjecture. Muslims hold it as revelation.

This website sets them side by side without blending them and without weakening either, and asks the reader only to notice what the Qur’an has done: it has refused the event on which the whole of Pauline theology is built, the atoning death, and it has done so in a book that confirms almost everything else the gospels say about him. The Gospel According to Islam tells the arrest, the trial and the aftermath in sections 25 to 27, with the Qur’anic text standing in the story where the gospels have the cross.
## Sources
- Ṭabarī, Jāmiʿ al-bayān, on 3:55 and 4:157-159.
- Mahmoud Ayoub, “Towards an Islamic Christology II: The Death of Jesus, Reality or Delusion?”, The Muslim World 70 (1980).
- Todd Lawson, The Crucifixion and the Qur’an: A Study in the History of Muslim Thought.
- Gabriel Said Reynolds, “The Muslim Jesus: Dead or Alive?”, Bulletin of the School of Oriental and African Studies 72 (2009).
- Irenaeus, Against Heresies 1.24.4, on Basilides; J. Arendzen, “Basilides”, The Catholic Encyclopedia, vol. 2 (1907), for the sources and dates.
- Lonsdale and Laura Ragg (eds.), The Gospel of Barnabas (Oxford, 1907), with the editors’ introduction on the date and provenance of the work.

title: The good news of Aḥmad
body: @islamic

Qur’an 61:6 is the verse in which ʿĪsā announces a messenger to come after him: “And when ʿĪsā son of Maryam said, ‘O Children of Israel, I am the messenger of God to you, confirming what came before me of the Torah, and giving good news of a messenger who will come after me, whose name is Aḥmad.’ But when he came to them with clear signs, they said, ‘This is plain sorcery.’” The verse states 3 things about him in one sentence: that he was sent to Israel, that he confirmed the Torah, and that he foretold another. Muslims and Christians have argued for 12 centuries over whether the gospels preserve the prophecy.
## Sent to Israel, confirming the Torah

The Qur’an is consistent that ʿĪsā was sent to the Children of Israel alone (3:49; 43:59; 61:6), and the gospels agree: “I was sent only to the lost sheep of the house of Israel” (Matthew 15:24); “Go nowhere among the gentiles” (Matthew 10:5-6). The mission to the gentiles was Paul of Tarsus’s, by his own account of his commission (Galatians 1:16; 2:7-9), and the first community disputed it (see James and the Jerusalem church).

The Qur’an is equally consistent that he confirmed the Torah (3:50; 5:46; 61:6), and so is Matthew: not one stroke of the law will pass (5:18). A messenger to Israel who confirmed the law is the Jesus of the earliest gospel tradition. The one who ended the law for all nations is the Christ of Paul of Tarsus.
## The good news of Aḥmad

Aḥmad, “most praised”, is from the same root as Muḥammad, “praised”, and Muslim tradition has always read the verse as foretelling him; the ḥadīth record Aḥmad among the Prophet’s names (Bukhārī, Book of the Virtues). The verse says that ʿĪsā gave this good news to Israel, and the Qur’an says elsewhere that the People of the Book find the Prophet “written with them in the Torah and the Injīl” (7:157) and recognise him “as they recognise their own sons” (2:146). The Qur’an’s claim, then, is that the Injīl given to ʿĪsā contained a prophecy of Muḥammad. Whether the four gospels still do is a separate question, and the Qur’an does not say that they do.
## The Paraclete

The earliest Muslim biography of the Prophet, by Ibn Isḥāq (d. 767), quotes John 15:23-27 in a Syriac-flavoured Arabic and identifies the Paraclete, whom Jesus promises will come after him, with Muḥammad; the passage is in Guillaume’s translation of Ibn Hishām, page 104. The argument has been made ever since.

In John 14-16 Jesus promises “another Paraclete” (paraklētos, advocate, helper, comforter) who will come when he has gone, who will teach the disciples all things, remind them of what he said, bear witness to him, convict the world of sin, guide them into all truth, not speak on his own but speak what he hears, and glorify him (14:16-17, 26; 15:26; 16:7-15). The Muslim case is that every one of these is said of Muḥammad in the Qur’an, and that a Paraclete who cannot come until Jesus goes (16:7) cannot be a spirit that was already present.
@consensus
Scholars of the New Testament identify the Paraclete with the Holy Spirit, because John 14:26 says so in as many words: “the Paraclete, the Holy Spirit, whom the Father will send in my name”.

A Muslim argument going back to the Middle Ages holds that the Greek originally read periklytos, “renowned, praised”, which translates Aḥmad, and that it was altered to paraklētos. No Greek manuscript of John has periklytos, and the word is not used elsewhere in the New Testament; the argument rests on the similarity of the words and on nothing in the textual record. This website does not use it.

The Christian reply in its classic form is Pfander’s, in the third part of The Balance of Truth (1829): the name is absent from the Gospel, the Paraclete is the Spirit, and the Qur’an’s claim came from “some apostate Christian”; the last is a guess without a source, and the rest is weighed on Pfander’s Balance of Truth.
## Where this page stands
The verse is the Qur’an’s own witness that ʿĪsā foretold a messenger, and Muslims hold it as revelation. Whether a trace of that prophecy survives in John’s Paraclete is a question of reading.

John calls his Paraclete the Holy Spirit, and the periklytos emendation has no manuscript support. John’s Paraclete also does things no spirit does: he speaks what he hears, he does not come until Jesus has gone, and the gospel calls him “another” of the same kind as Jesus, which is to say a person. Readers may weigh that for themselves.

This website relies on the Qur’an’s plain statement, and on the plain fact that the gospels record a Jesus who spoke of one to come after him. The Gospel According to Islam gives the promise in section 24, with the Qur’anic passage “Jesus Prophesied the Coming of Muhammad” standing in the text.
## Sources

- Raymond Brown, The Gospel According to John XIII-XXI, Anchor Bible, appendix on the Paraclete.
- Ṭabarī and Ibn Kathīr, commentary on 61:6 and 7:157.
